- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later — suggest adjusting for a downward bias after initial spikes.
- When true values show sharp downward trends (e.g., after 85–90 range), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “mean reversion” penalty to forecasts above 85–88.
- Forecasts tend to be too high when history includes recent high values (e.g., >90) — reduce forecast by 1–3% relative to recent peak.
- Model underestimates when true values are clustered near 80–82 — adjust downward by 0.5–1.5 units if recent history is below 85.
- Overshoots after sharp spikes (e.g., 90+ to 85+) are common — apply a “lag correction” by subtracting 1–2 units from forecast if prior day was a spike.
- Forecast mean is often 1–2 units higher than true mean — apply a global downward shift of 0.5–1.0 units for all forecasts.
- When true values show strong downward momentum (e.g., 85→80), model fails to anticipate — add a “momentum decay” rule: if 3 consecutive days are falling, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0 per day.
